title: Combinations (order does not matter)
quickIdea: Choosing a set, not arranging a sequence. C(n,r) = n!/(r!(n-r)!), and C(n,r) = C(n,n-r).
remember: C(n,r) = n! / (r! (n-r)!) counts r-subsets of an n-set.
C(n,r) = C(n,n-r) - use the smaller side for arithmetic.
Vandermonde: C(m+n,r) = sum over k of C(m,k) C(n,r-k).
Sum of all subsets: C(n,0) + ... + C(n,n) = 2^n.
Gap template: arrange the blockers first, then choose gaps for the rest.

example.prompt: A committee of 12 from 10 men and 10 women, exactly 6 of each.
example.work: Choose 6 of the 10 men and 6 of the 10 women; independent choices multiply.

gateAngle: Two moves cover most GATE combination questions: multiply independent choices (committee questions), and use the gap template for 'no two adjacent' (GATE 1999 Q.1.3: C(n+1,k)).

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A committee of 12 from 10 men and 10 women must contain an even number of women. How many committees?
variations.why: Sum over the feasible even cases k = 2,4,6,8,10 of C(10,k)C(10,12-k). k = 0 is infeasible because it needs 12 men. The sum is 45 + 9450 + 44100 + 9450 + 45 = 63090, not half of C(20,12) = 62985.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why is C(n,2) = n(n-1)/2 the same as the number of handshakes among n people?
variations.answer: Each unordered pair is one handshake
variations.why: Ordered pairs give n(n-1); dividing by 2! removes the ordering. The division is legal because every unordered pair was counted exactly twice.

trap.what: Using a combination when the question silently assigns roles.
trap.why: If the chosen people get distinct posts (chair, secretary), order has entered the problem and you must multiply by the number of role assignments.
trap.counterexample: Choosing a 3-person committee from 10: C(10,3) = 120. Choosing a chair, secretary and treasurer from 10: P(10,3) = 720 = 120 x 3!.

check.question: How many 3-element subsets does a 10-element set have?
